Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Rohan still remembers the day the tsunami hit his family's coastal town in Thailand. He was 17 then, and the sounds of screams, crashing waves, and crumbling buildings are etched in his mind like a scar. The memory feels so extreme that it's hard for him to believe it actually happened to him – as if he's watching a movie of someone else's life. When it resurfaces, he can almost taste the saltwater and debris that filled his mouth as he struggled to stay afloat. The event has left an indelible mark on Rohan's life. He recalls feeling a searing pain in his neck as he clung to a piece of wreckage, which has since become a persistent somatic ache – a constant reminder of that day. Whenever the memory returns, the pain flares up, and he feels physically unwell, as if his body is reliving the trauma all over again. As a UX designer, Rohan spends most of his time staring at screens and typing away on his keyboard. However, the slightest twinge in his neck can send him spiraling into a vortex of anxiety and dread. He becomes withdrawn and isolated, unable to shake off the feeling that he's living on borrowed time – that another disaster is just around the corner, waiting to strike. Rohan has started to distrust others, wondering if they're genuinely concerned about his well-being or just pretending to be. He feels like an outsider, as if he no longer belongs in the world of the living. His relationships have suffered as a result; he's become increasingly withdrawn and isolated, pushing away friends and family who try to get close to him. The trauma-related events that Rohan experienced during the tsunami – the sounds, sights, and smells – continue to haunt him. Sometimes, he'll catch a whiff of saltwater or hear a distant rumble of thunder, and the full emotional intensity of the event will come flooding back without any clear image or memory. It's as if his body has become a repository for the trauma, storing it away in muscle memory and waiting to unleash it at a moment's notice. Rohan's sense of isolation has become so profound that he feels like he no longer belongs anywhere – not even in his own skin. He's started to question his identity and purpose, wondering if he's just going through the motions of life without any real direction or meaning. Lately, Rohan has found it increasingly difficult to concentrate on his work. The neck pain has become a constant distraction, and he's started to experience vivid flashbacks during meetings and presentations. His performance has suffered as a result, and he's worried that he'll lose his job if he doesn't get his symptoms under control. It was only when Rohan had a panic attack in front of his colleagues – triggered by the sound of a fire alarm – that he realized he needed help. He's afraid that if he doesn't address these issues, they'll consume him whole, leaving him a shell of his former self. As he sits in the therapist's office, he's hoping to find a way to reclaim his life and learn to trust himself and others again.
